title: Trace the water, drop the trickles
allegory: Circuit pruning is like mapping a river delta backwards from the sea: for every stream, work out what share of the water reaching the sea passed through it by any route, then erase the streams that carry only a trickle.
map: streams and junctions of the delta
nodes (tokens, features, error terms, logits) and weighted edges
the share of a junction's water from each inflow
water reaching the sea by any route: direct, via one junction, via two
total influence: A + A² + A³ + ..., the Neumann series
water only runs downhill, so every route ends
no backward edges: A is nilpotent and the series terminates
erasing streams that carry only a trickle
pruning nodes and edges whose influence falls below a threshold

chapters.name: Too many streams
chapters.note: which of these made it say Austin?

props.label: every feature that fired, every link
...the capital of the state containing Dallas is

cap.1: You've drawn every feature that fired on one prompt and every link between them. It's a hairball. Which pieces actually produced the answer?
cap.2: An attribution graph has nodes for tokens, transcoder latents, error terms and output logits, joined by weighted edges. Even with sparse latents there are far too many to read.
cap.3: The raw graph is a dense DAG over one prompt. Pruning keeps the subgraph that carries most of the influence on the output logits, small enough to read and to test.

cap.1: Think of a river delta. Water from many springs splits and merges on its way to the sea. To see what feeds the sea, follow the water, not the maze.
cap.2: Features are junctions, edges are streams, and the answer is the sea. What you want is the share of the answer that flowed through each junction, by any route.
cap.3: Influence on the output is a path sum: products of normalised edge weights along each path, summed over all paths. Nodes and edges with small path-summed influence get pruned.

cap.1: Add the water arriving directly, then via one junction, then via two, and so on. Because water only runs downhill, the list of routes runs out.
cap.2: With A the normalised adjacency matrix, A² counts two-step paths and A³ three-step ones; summing the powers gives total influence. That's the compute_influence exercise.
cap.3: Total influence = Σ_{k≥1} Aᵏ = (I − A)⁻¹ − I. A transformer's graph has no backward edges, so A is nilpotent and the Neumann series terminates exactly.

cap.1: Along one route, shares multiply; across routes, they add. Dallas feeds all of Texas, Texas feeds 0.6 of Austin: 0.6 that way, plus 0.1 direct, makes 0.7.
cap.2: Illustrative weights on the real Dallas-Texas-Austin shape. Multiply along a path, add across paths: Dallas reaches 'say Austin' with 0.1 direct plus 1.0 × 0.6 via Texas.
cap.3: (A²)[austin, dallas] = Σ_j A[austin, j]·A[j, dallas] is the two-hop term; the Neumann sum adds every hop count. A node's influence on the logits reads off the total-influence matrix.

chapters.name: Tidy is not true

left.title: a tidy pruned graph
lines: much input quietly from error nodes

right.title: a trustworthy one
lines: swap in another state: answer follows?
only then call it a circuit

chapters.verdict: Pruning makes a graph readable, not true. Check completeness, then intervene.

cap.1: Erasing trickles makes a clean map, but a clean map can still mislead. Some water comes from springs you never charted: the parts the features don't explain.
cap.2: Error nodes hold what the transcoders fail to explain. Report completeness, the share of input from features and embeddings rather than errors, and test the pruned graph by ablating a supernode.
cap.3: Pruning optimises readability, not faithfulness. A graph is a hypothesis: zero-ablate a supernode or swap features across prompts and check the output moves the way the graph predicts.

cap.1: Where do you stop erasing? Keep more of the water and the map fills with streams; keep less and you may erase one that mattered. There's no perfect line.
cap.2: Illustrative trade-off. Current method: influence-threshold pruning on a local replacement model, one prompt at a time. Open: the cut is a judgement call and attention is frozen, not explained. What you need: prune, then test.
cap.3: The replacement is linear only given fixed feature activations and frozen attention patterns, so each graph is a local, per-prompt hypothesis. The threshold trades readability against completeness.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: From hairball to a circuit you can read
A pruned graph is a hypothesis: ablate it

cap.1: Pruning turns an unreadable tangle into a few paths you can follow and test. That's how you learn what a model actually did on one prompt.
cap.2: Readable attribution graphs showed Claude 3.5 Haiku doing two-step inference, Dallas to Texas to Austin, and planning rhymes ahead: claims you can only make, and check, with a graph you can intervene on.
cap.3: Influence-based pruning localises a computation to a few supernodes you can ablate or swap: the step that makes attribution graphs usable for understanding and steering models.

coda.title: Set the flows, then move the cut

params.label: share of 'say Austin' fed by Texas

readouts.label: kept at this cut-off
readouts.f: ['Dallas', 'Texas', 'capital', 'say a capital', 'error node'].filter((n, i) => [(1 - t - e)*0.25 + t, t, (1 - t - e)*0.75, (1 - t - e)*0.75, e][i] >= max(tau, 0.001)).join(', ') || 'nothing'

caption.1: Set how much of 'say Austin' flows through Texas and how much from unexplained error, then raise the cut-off. Watch which pieces survive.
caption.2: Bars are influence on the output. Dallas gets its direct share plus everything via Texas; 'capital' matters only through 'say a capital'. Raise the error share: completeness drops, however tidy the graph.
caption.3: Toy: influence = direct weight + products along paths. Pruning keeps nodes at or above τ; completeness = 1 − error share. A high τ can leave a clean graph that explains little.

Supply chains: which upstream parts most shape the final product, by any route

hamming.what: Scoring every node and edge of an attribution graph by its total influence on the output, summed over all paths, and dropping those below a threshold.
hamming.when: Right after building an attribution graph for one prompt, before you try to read it or test it with ablations.
hamming.why: A raw graph is far too big to read; keeping what carries most of the influence turns it into a small, testable hypothesis about how the model got its answer.

object.title: The influence ledger
object.subtitle: Seven pieces of one prompt's graph: their direct link to the answer, their influence by every route, and what survives the cut.

cap.1: Seven pieces of one prompt. Left: each one's direct link to 'say Austin'. Middle: its influence by every route. Right: what survives the cut.
cap.2: Illustrative numbers. Rows are nodes; columns are the direct edge weight into the output, total influence from the Neumann sum, and influence after thresholding.
cap.3: Illustrative normalised graph: column 1 is A[out, j], column 2 is (A + A² + A³)[out, j], column 3 is column 2 thresholded at τ.

cap.1: Look at 'capital': no direct link to the answer at all, yet a big share of influence by other routes. Direct links undersell it.
cap.2: A node with zero direct weight can carry large total influence through intermediates, which is why you sum over paths.
cap.3: capital has A[out, capital] = 0 but total influence 0.38 through intermediates such as 'say a capital' and 'state': multi-hop paths are its whole contribution.

cap.1: Raise the cut and the small pieces vanish from the right-hand column. What's left is the circuit you'll read.
cap.2: At τ = 0.15, misc and error drop out; Dallas, capital, state, Texas and 'say a capital' remain.
cap.3: Thresholding node influence yields the pruned subgraph; edges are pruned by their own influence scores too.

cap.1: Cut harder and only a few pieces remain. Tidier, but you've erased a route that carried real water. The cut is a choice.
cap.2: A strict threshold keeps a clean story at the cost of completeness: the dropped routes still contributed.
cap.3: Readability and completeness trade off monotonically in τ; choose the cut to answer your question, then validate by ablation.

cap.1: Notice the error row: it vanished at the cut, but its share of the answer didn't. Report it rather than hiding it.
cap.2: Pruning can drop error nodes from view; completeness still records how much input they supplied.
cap.3: Completeness, the share of input from feature and embedding nodes rather than error nodes, should be reported alongside any pruned graph.

predict.q: Why does the sum A + A² + A³ + ... stop?

options.t: No backward edges: A is nilpotent

predict.why: A transformer's graph is acyclic, so some power of A is exactly zero and the Neumann series terminates.

predict.q: Your graph has no edges between token positions at all. What went wrong?

options.t: You froze the whole attention output instead of just the pattern
The pruning cut-off is too high

predict.why: Attention's value path is the only route between positions: freeze only hook_pattern and keep V·W_O differentiable.

predict.q: Your pruned graph is clean, but completeness is low. What does that mean?

options.t: Much of the input comes from error nodes: it explains less than it seems

predict.why: Completeness is the share of input from features and embeddings rather than errors.

object.where: Anywhere influence flows through a network by many routes: supply chains, citation graphs, economic input-output tables.
